From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.

## Executive view

The Seller’s package is materially seller-favourable. The principal concerns are:

1. **Bluefen consent is not yet obtained**, despite representing about 30% of FY26 revenue.
2. **Riverlark debt and security would remain at Completion**, contrary to a debt-free/cash-free acquisition.
3. **Ownership of the Ironquay IP is not established.**
4. **Completion bonuses and related on-costs are omitted from funds flow.**
5. **The export/privacy incident is unresolved.**
6. The Seller seeks to apply a **low cap, short limitation period, deductible basket, constructive buyer knowledge, blanket disclosure, non-reliance and exclusive-remedy provisions across virtually every type of claim**, including title and capacity.

We should not accept these positions without significant changes.

---

## 1. Bluefen consent — material Completion risk

Bluefen accounts for approximately **AUD 3.6 million, or 30% of FY26 revenue**. No final consent has been provided, and the disclosure expressly says there is no evidence that the conditions in clause 11.3 have been satisfied.

The Seller’s proposal that the condition is satisfied merely by delivering written consent is inadequate if that consent:

- remains conditional;
- requires payments, amendments or concessions;
- can be withdrawn;
- imposes adverse commercial terms; or
- does not fully waive the relevant change-of-control rights.

### Buyer position

Make this a genuine condition precedent requiring:

- final, unconditional and irrevocable written consent;
- satisfaction or written waiver of all associated conditions;
- no material amendment, price concession, payment or other obligation without Buyer consent;
- evidence reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer; and
- confirmation that Completion will not cause termination, suspension or renegotiation rights.

The Buyer should have a termination right if this is not achieved by the long-stop date. The Seller must not be able to “deem” the condition satisfied.

---

## 2. Riverlark debt and security — must be released at Completion

The proposed post-Completion release is unacceptable. Approximately **AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding**, and the facility includes security and change-of-control provisions.

A post-Completion release could leave the Buyer owning a company whose assets remain secured for Seller-period debt. It also contradicts the agreed **debt-free/cash-free** basis.

### Buyer position

Require, as simultaneous Completion deliverables:

- a binding payout letter;
- repayment from the Seller’s Completion proceeds, not additional Buyer funds;
- executed releases of all guarantees and security;
- control of any registrations or documents needed to discharge PPSR and other registrations;
- discharge undertakings acceptable to the Buyer; and
- confirmation that no break fees, accrued interest or other facility amounts remain with the Company.

All Riverlark amounts, including interest, fees and discharge costs, should be treated as **Debt** and reduce the amount paid to the Seller.

---

## 3. Ironquay IP — payment indemnity does not establish ownership

The Company’s ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on payment of all SOW3 fees. The records identify **AUD 180,000 as open**, and there is no receipt, independent confirmation or confirmatory assignment.

An indemnity limited to the outstanding payment does not cure the central risk: the Company may not own IP required to operate the business. The resulting loss could materially exceed AUD 180,000.

### Buyer position

Before Completion require:

- confirmation from Ironquay that all amounts have been paid;
- an effective assignment of all relevant IP and Project Materials;
- delivery of source materials, credentials and associated documentation;
- appropriate moral-rights consents; and
- confirmation that Ironquay retains no lien, termination right or adverse licence right.

If this cannot be completed before closing, require an escrow or holdback and a specific indemnity covering **all loss arising from defective ownership, use or exploitation of the relevant IP**, not merely the SOW3 invoice.

---

## 4. Completion bonuses — Seller transaction expense omitted from funds flow

The **AUD 420,000 Completion-triggered bonuses** are a direct consequence of the sale. The actual liability may be higher once payroll tax, superannuation, PAYG and other employment on-costs are determined.

Omitting them from funds flow risks the Company—and therefore the Buyer—funding Seller transaction costs after Completion.

### Buyer position

Treat the bonuses and all related taxes and on-costs as:

- Seller transaction expenses or debt-like items;
- deducted dollar-for-dollar from the amount payable to the Seller; and
- paid or fully provided for at Completion.

Require a schedule of recipients, conditions, gross amounts and on-costs, plus a Seller indemnity for any excess or omitted liability.

---

## 5. Export/privacy incident — unresolved, not merely operational

The export may contain approximately 1,240 records and was sent to an unintended external email address. The investigation does not establish who accessed it, its precise contents, whether containment succeeded or whether notification is required.

Business email addresses and associated role/activity data may constitute personal information. Potential consequences include investigation and remediation costs, notifications, regulator action, contractual claims, customer impact and reputational loss.

The absence of a current quantified loss does not make the matter immaterial.

### Buyer position

Require before Completion:

- a properly documented forensic investigation;
- identification of the recipient and evidence of deletion/non-access where available;
- confirmation of the affected data and individuals;
- legal assessment of notification obligations;
- preservation and notification of relevant cyber insurance;
- details of all customer, regulator and third-party communications; and
- an agreed remediation plan.

Seek a specific indemnity for all pre-Completion circumstances connected with the incident, including investigation, remediation, notification, regulatory and third-party costs. It should sit outside the general cap, basket and 18-month period.

Also require an interim covenant preventing communications or admissions to regulators, customers or affected persons without consultation with the Buyer, except where legally required.

---

## 6. Liability cap — too broad and too low if applied as proposed

A **20% cap (AUD 4.8 million)** may be negotiable for ordinary business warranties depending on the overall risk allocation, but it should not apply to every claim.

The Seller proposes applying the same cap to title, capacity, indemnities and other claims. That is unacceptable. If the Seller does not own the shares or cannot validly sell them, the Buyer could lose substantially all of its AUD 24 million investment while recovering only AUD 4.8 million.

### Buyer position

At minimum:

- **ordinary warranties:** negotiate a higher cap, ideally 30–50% of price, subject to the rest of the package;
- **title, capacity and authority:** 100% of the purchase price;
- **purchase-price adjustments, debt claims and payment obligations:** full recovery;
- **specific indemnities:** separate negotiated caps or uncapped where appropriate;
- **fraud, fraudulent concealment, deliberate breach and wilful misconduct:** uncapped;
- **tax:** separate tax covenant/indemnity, ordinarily with a materially higher cap;
- **core IP risk:** outside the ordinary warranty cap or subject to a higher separate cap.

“Aggregate liability” drafting should also avoid counting amounts recovered from insurance or third parties as Seller liability unless they actually reduce the Buyer’s loss.

---

## 7. De minimis and basket — deductible structure favours Seller

The proposed thresholds are:

- AUD 25,000 per claim; and
- AUD 250,000 aggregate basket, with only the excess recoverable.

The basket is approximately 1% of the purchase price and is structured as a **deductible**, meaning the Buyer permanently bears the first AUD 250,000 of otherwise valid loss.

### Buyer position

Push for:

- a lower de minimis;
- aggregation of related claims or claims arising from the same facts;
- a lower basket; and
- a **tipping basket**, so that once the basket is reached the Buyer recovers the full amount.

No de minimis or basket should apply to title, capacity, tax, specific indemnities, price adjustments, debt, leakage, fraud or deliberate breach.

---

## 8. Time limits — 18 months is too short and cannot apply to all claims

An 18-month period may expire before latent issues emerge or before a full audit cycle has been completed. It is plainly inappropriate for title, tax, IP ownership, indemnities and continuing obligations.

### Buyer position

Seek:

- ordinary warranties: at least **24–36 months**;
- tax claims: until the applicable statutory review period expires, plus an agreed buffer;
- title and capacity: at least six years or the applicable statutory period;
- specific indemnities: tailored periods linked to final resolution of the relevant risk;
- covenants and payment obligations: the ordinary legal limitation period.

A claim should be preserved by a good-faith notice identifying its general nature. Failure to include precise quantum or full particulars should not invalidate it. Any requirement to commence proceedings after notice should allow sufficient time and preserve contingent or third-party claims.

---

## 9. Blanket data-room and public-register disclosure — should be rejected

Clauses 1.1 and 1.2 attempt to disclose every matter contained or referred to anywhere in the data room, Accounts, statutory registers and public records.

That shifts the burden to the Buyer to locate and interpret every possible inconsistency. It may also permit an obscure or incomplete document to qualify a warranty even where the commercial significance was not apparent.

### Buyer position

Only matters **fairly disclosed** should qualify warranties. “Fairly disclosed” should require enough detail to identify:

- the nature and scope of the matter;
- the relevant facts and documents;
- its reasonably apparent impact; and
- the specific warranty being qualified.

General disclosure should be deleted or heavily limited. Public records should not be generally disclosed merely because they are searchable. Each disclosure should be specific and cross-referenced to the relevant warranty.

The disclosure letter is also dated by reference to the data room as at **22 September 2026**. It is stale for a November transaction process. Require:

- a final indexed data-room copy;
- identification of documents added, amended or removed;
- an updated disclosure letter immediately before signing or Completion; and
- a warranty bring-down at Completion.

The “no admission” language does not make an otherwise inadequate disclosure effective.

---

## 10. Buyer knowledge — constructive and adviser knowledge should be removed

The Seller seeks to bar claims for anything the Buyer or its advisers knew or could have discovered from the data room or public records. This is an extremely broad constructive-knowledge standard and undermines the warranties.

Warranties are intended to allocate risk and elicit disclosure, not merely repeat due diligence findings.

### Buyer position

Prefer no general buyer-knowledge exclusion. If one must be accepted:

- restrict it to the actual, conscious knowledge of a small list of named senior Buyer personnel;
- exclude advisers and other representatives;
- exclude constructive, imputed or deemed knowledge;
- impose no duty to investigate;
- delete “discoverable from” language;
- place the burden of proving knowledge on the Seller; and
- provide that knowledge does not limit specific indemnities, title/capacity claims, fraud or matters the Seller failed to disclose fairly.

---

## 11. Non-reliance, exclusive remedy and “all Claims” language

The Seller seeks to apply the contractual limitations to all claims regardless of legal basis. This could restrict claims concerning pre-contractual misrepresentations, indemnities, covenants, equitable relief and statutory misleading or deceptive conduct.

### Buyer position

Limit the exclusive-remedy regime to ordinary warranty claims. Expressly preserve:

- fraud and fraudulent concealment;
- wilful misconduct and deliberate breach;
- misleading or deceptive conduct and non-excludable statutory rights;
- specific indemnities;
- purchase-price adjustments;
- debt and payment claims;
- breach of pre- and post-Completion covenants;
- specific performance, injunctions and other equitable relief;
- rights under ancillary documents; and
- claims concerning title, capacity and authority.

The agreement should also prohibit double recovery without extinguishing legitimate concurrent causes of action.

---

## 12. Tax and IP should not simply fall within the general regime

Tax and IP are potentially high-severity areas and do not fit an 18-month, 20%-cap, deductible-basket regime.

### Buyer position

Require:

- a separate tax covenant or tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax;
- comprehensive tax warranties;
- survival through the relevant statutory review periods;
- protection for payroll tax and superannuation connected with the bonuses;
- robust IP ownership, validity, non-infringement, open-source, employee/contractor assignment and cybersecurity warranties; and
- a higher cap or specific protection for core IP ownership issues.

---

## 13. Title evidence is insufficient by itself

The share register is important evidence but does not alone establish clean legal and beneficial title. It does not rule out security interests, equitable interests, options, rights to issue shares or defective historic issuances.

### Buyer position

Require:

- warranties of legal and beneficial ownership;
- transfer free of all encumbrances and third-party rights;
- confirmation of the complete issued capital and absence of options or conversion rights;
- original share certificates or agreed lost-certificate procedures;
- executed share transfers and updated registers at Completion;
- relevant ASIC and PPSR searches;
- releases of any security affecting the shares; and
- a 100% purchase-price cap for title and capacity claims.

---

## 14. Supplier renewals

The Seller’s description of the three **AUD 110,000 renewals** as ordinary-course costs is not enough. The disclosures do not establish whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or consistent with prior practice.

### Buyer position

Review the renewal contracts and require clarity on:

- renewal dates and service periods;
- termination rights;
- prepayments and accruals;
- price increases or unusual terms;
- whether commitments were made outside ordinary course; and
- treatment under working-capital, debt-like-item or locked-box provisions.

The Seller should not enter into or vary material supplier commitments between signing and Completion without Buyer consent.

---

## 15. Office lease and Mossvale

The current disclosures suggest an office lease notification obligation and a Mossvale assignment restriction. A share sale does not necessarily constitute an assignment, but the complete contracts must be reviewed for separate change-of-control provisions or indirect-transfer language.

### Buyer position

Require the Seller to:

- identify and comply with all applicable notice requirements;
- confirm whether any change-of-control right exists;
- deliver evidence of required notices or consents; and
- warrant that Completion will not cause termination, default, acceleration, price changes or loss of rights.

---

## 16. Price mechanics and Completion protection

The statement that funds flow “reflects the agreed price mechanics” should not be accepted without a complete reconciliation. At least AUD 3.2 million of bank debt, AUD 420,000 plus on-costs of transaction bonuses, and potentially AUD 180,000 of Ironquay liability require express treatment.

### Buyer position

Obtain a complete sources-and-uses statement and define comprehensively:

- Debt;
- cash;
- transaction expenses;
- leakage;
- employee liabilities;
- unpaid tax and payroll liabilities;
- accrued interest and break costs;
- security discharge costs; and
- any working-capital adjustment.

Require:

- a Seller-certified Completion statement;
- a dollar-for-dollar adjustment mechanism;
- post-Completion verification and dispute procedures;
- no leakage covenant where a locked-box is used; and
- sufficient escrow, holdback or other credit support.

The Seller’s ability to meet claims should also be assessed. If Harbourglass is a holding vehicle that may distribute the sale proceeds, contractual claims may have little practical value without an escrow, retention, guarantee or warranty and indemnity insurance solution.

---

# Recommended negotiation priorities

## Deal blockers before Completion

1. Obtain unconditional Bluefen consent with all conditions satisfied or waived.
2. Repay Riverlark and release all security simultaneously at Completion.
3. Establish clean ownership of the Ironquay IP.
4. Deduct Completion bonuses and all on-costs from Seller proceeds.
5. Complete the privacy/export investigation and agree a specific indemnity.

## Core SPA changes

6. Restrict the 20% cap to ordinary warranties and negotiate a higher general cap.
7. Apply a 100% cap and longer survival to title and capacity.
8. Carve tax, specific indemnities, price adjustments, fraud, deliberate breach and key IP matters out of the general limitations.
9. Extend ordinary warranty survival to 24–36 months and use tailored periods for other claims.
10. Replace the deductible basket with a lower tipping basket and narrow the de minimis.
11. Delete blanket data-room/public-register disclosure and require fair, specific disclosure.
12. Delete constructive and adviser knowledge; at most accept actual knowledge of named Buyer personnel.
13. Narrow exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses and preserve statutory, indemnity, covenant and equitable claims.
14. Reconcile all debt-like items and transaction expenses through Completion funds flow.
15. Obtain updated disclosures, warranty bring-downs and adequate recourse security.

Overall, the Seller’s draft does not presently provide an acceptable risk allocation for a **AUD 24 million debt-free/cash-free acquisition**. The unresolved consent, secured debt, IP and privacy matters should be solved through Completion deliverables and specific indemnities, rather than being pushed into a heavily restricted general warranty regime.

## 9. Blanket data-room and public-register disclosure — should be rejected

Clauses 1.1 and 1.2 attempt to disclose every matter contained or referred to anywhere in the data room, Accounts, statutory registers and public records.

That shifts the burden to the Buyer to locate and interpret every possible inconsistency. It may also permit an obscure or incomplete document to qualify a warranty even where the commercial significance was not apparent.

### Buyer position

Only matters **fairly disclosed** should qualify warranties. “Fairly disclosed” should require enough detail to identify:

- the nature and scope of the matter;
- the relevant facts and documents;
- its reasonably apparent impact; and
- the specific warranty being qualified.

General disclosure should be deleted or heavily limited. Public records should not be generally disclosed merely because they are searchable. Each disclosure should be specific and cross-referenced to the relevant warranty.

The disclosure letter is also dated by reference to the data room as at **22 September 2026**. It is stale for a November transaction process. Require:

- a final indexed data-room copy;
- identification of documents added, amended or removed;
- an updated disclosure letter immediately before signing or Completion; and
- a warranty bring-down at Completion.

The “no admission” language does not make an otherwise inadequate disclosure effective.

---

## 10. Buyer knowledge — constructive and adviser knowledge should be removed

The Seller seeks to bar claims for anything the Buyer or its advisers knew or could have discovered from the data room or public records. This is an extremely broad constructive-knowledge standard and undermines the warranties.

Warranties are intended to allocate risk and elicit disclosure, not merely repeat due diligence findings.

### Buyer position

Prefer no general buyer-knowledge exclusion. If one must be accepted:

- restrict it to the actual, conscious knowledge of a small list of named senior Buyer personnel;
- exclude advisers and other representatives;
- exclude constructive, imputed or deemed knowledge;
- impose no duty to investigate;
- delete “discoverable from” language;
- place the burden of proving knowledge on the Seller; and
- provide that knowledge does not limit specific indemnities, title/capacity claims, fraud or matters the Seller failed to disclose fairly.

---

## 11. Non-reliance, exclusive remedy and “all Claims” language

The Seller seeks to apply the contractual limitations to all claims regardless of legal basis. This could restrict claims concerning pre-contractual misrepresentations, indemnities, covenants, equitable relief and statutory misleading or deceptive conduct.

### Buyer position

Limit the exclusive-remedy regime to ordinary warranty claims. Expressly preserve:

- fraud and fraudulent concealment;
- wilful misconduct and deliberate breach;
- misleading or deceptive conduct and non-excludable statutory rights;
- specific indemnities;
- purchase-price adjustments;
- debt and payment claims;
- breach of pre- and post-Completion covenants;
- specific performance, injunctions and other equitable relief;
- rights under ancillary documents; and
- claims concerning title, capacity and authority.

The agreement should also prohibit double recovery without extinguishing legitimate concurrent causes of action.

---

## 12. Tax and IP should not simply fall within the general regime

Tax and IP are potentially high-severity areas and do not fit an 18-month, 20%-cap, deductible-basket regime.

### Buyer position

Require:

- a separate tax covenant or tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax;
- comprehensive tax warranties;
- survival through the relevant statutory review periods;
- protection for payroll tax and superannuation connected with the bonuses;
- robust IP ownership, validity, non-infringement, open-source, employee/contractor assignment and cybersecurity warranties; and
- a higher cap or specific protection for core IP ownership issues.

---

## 13. Title evidence is insufficient by itself

The share register is important evidence but does not alone establish clean legal and beneficial title. It does not rule out security interests, equitable interests, options, rights to issue shares or defective historic issuances.

### Buyer position

Require:

- warranties of legal and beneficial ownership;
- transfer free of all encumbrances and third-party rights;
- confirmation of the complete issued capital and absence of options or conversion rights;
- original share certificates or agreed lost-certificate procedures;
- executed share transfers and updated registers at Completion;
- relevant ASIC and PPSR searches;
- releases of any security affecting the shares; and
- a 100% purchase-price cap for title and capacity claims.

---

## 14. Supplier renewals

The Seller’s description of the three **AUD 110,000 renewals** as ordinary-course costs is not enough. The disclosures do not establish whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or consistent with prior practice.

### Buyer position

Review the renewal contracts and require clarity on:

- renewal dates and service periods;
- termination rights;
- prepayments and accruals;
- price increases or unusual terms;
- whether commitments were made outside ordinary course; and
- treatment under working-capital, debt-like-item or locked-box provisions.

The Seller should not enter into or vary material supplier commitments between signing and Completion without Buyer consent.

---

## 15. Office lease and Mossvale

The current disclosures suggest an office lease notification obligation and a Mossvale assignment restriction. A share sale does not necessarily constitute an assignment, but the complete contracts must be reviewed for separate change-of-control provisions or indirect-transfer language.

### Buyer position

Require the Seller to:

- identify and comply with all applicable notice requirements;
- confirm whether any change-of-control right exists;
- deliver evidence of required notices or consents; and
- warrant that Completion will not cause termination, default, acceleration, price changes or loss of rights.

---

## 16. Price mechanics and Completion protection

The statement that funds flow “reflects the agreed price mechanics” should not be accepted without a complete reconciliation. At least AUD 3.2 million of bank debt, AUD 420,000 plus on-costs of transaction bonuses, and potentially AUD 180,000 of Ironquay liability require express treatment.

### Buyer position

Obtain a complete sources-and-uses statement and define comprehensively:

- Debt;
- cash;
- transaction expenses;
- leakage;
- employee liabilities;
- unpaid tax and payroll liabilities;
- accrued interest and break costs;
- security discharge costs; and
- any working-capital adjustment.

Require:

- a Seller-certified Completion statement;
- a dollar-for-dollar adjustment mechanism;
- post-Completion verification and dispute procedures;
- no leakage covenant where a locked-box is used; and
- sufficient escrow, holdback or other credit support.

The Seller’s ability to meet claims should also be assessed. If Harbourglass is a holding vehicle that may distribute the sale proceeds, contractual claims may have little practical value without an escrow, retention, guarantee or warranty and indemnity insurance solution.

# Recommended negotiation priorities

## Deal blockers before Completion

1. Obtain unconditional Bluefen consent with all conditions satisfied or waived.
2. Repay Riverlark and release all security simultaneously at Completion.
3. Establish clean ownership of the Ironquay IP.
4. Deduct Completion bonuses and all on-costs from Seller proceeds.
5. Complete the privacy/export investigation and agree a specific indemnity.

## Core SPA changes

6. Restrict the 20% cap to ordinary warranties and negotiate a higher general cap.
7. Apply a 100% cap and longer survival to title and capacity.
8. Carve tax, specific indemnities, price adjustments, fraud, deliberate breach and key IP matters out of the general limitations.
9. Extend ordinary warranty survival to 24–36 months and use tailored periods for other claims.
10. Replace the deductible basket with a lower tipping basket and narrow the de minimis.
11. Delete blanket data-room/public-register disclosure and require fair, specific disclosure.
12. Delete constructive and adviser knowledge; at most accept actual knowledge of named Buyer personnel.
13. Narrow exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses and preserve statutory, indemnity, covenant and equitable claims.
14. Reconcile all debt-like items and transaction expenses through Completion funds flow.
15. Obtain updated disclosures, warranty bring-downs and adequate recourse security.

Overall, the Seller’s draft does not presently provide an acceptable risk allocation for a **AUD 24 million debt-free/cash-free acquisition**. The unresolved consent, secured debt, IP and privacy matters should be solved through Completion deliverables and specific indemnities, rather than being pushed into a heavily restricted general warranty regime.
